what: A replay of one Design Studio run: Can a mouse grow wings that actually support its flight?
live_hint: studio-live.html polls POST /tool/session_read on a running sim-engine/http.mjs and shows that instead when it answers. Start one with: node sim-engine/http.mjs
question: Can a mouse grow wings that actually support its flight?
verdict: The question as asked is not answerable by this repository, and the system says so instead of answering a nearby question it can do. An area check cannot settle a power question; what is missing is a lift coefficient measured through a wingbeat and a flight-muscle power density for the clade.

entries.author: agent:flying-mouse
entries.body: generation 1: Generation 0 refused "wing" and named what it does allow here: the styliform cartilage and the styliform element, the wrist strut that tensions a gliding membrane. So name the mammalian glider outright -- a patagium AND a styliform cartilage -- and see which half the ontology will give. Then declare the three quantities the aerodynamics needs, each with a source saying it is a design input and not a measurement.

entries.author: agent:flying-mouse
entries.body: asked for a patagium and a styliform cartilage, the ontology gives one and refuses the other: styliform cartilage is in the hierarchy, and patagium, wing are never_in_taxon Glires. A mouse may have the strut that tensions a flight membrane and may not have the membrane. That is the shape of the whole result: the skeleton of flight is permitted in this clade and the surface that would carry the air is not.

entries.author: agent:flying-mouse
entries.body: At no corner of the stated ranges does lift reach the weight: the best case is 0.388x, which is short by a factor of 2.58. To carry 0.015-0.03 kg at 2-3 m/s the area needed is 180.3 cm2 against the 70.0 cm2 stated; equivalently the speed needed at the stated area is 4.81 m/s.

detail.C_Lmax_source: Bishop KL 2007, Aerodynamic force generation, performance and control of body orientation during gliding in sugar gliders (Petaurus breviceps), J Exp Biol 210:2593-2606
detail.C_Lmax_caveat: THIS IS A STALLED-MEMBRANE GLIDE COEFFICIENT, NOT A STEADY-FLIGHT MAXIMUM, and the source is explicit that it was not enough. In the same glides the animals accelerated downward at 1.0 +/- 0.5 m/s2 and forward at 2.1 +/- 0.6 m/s2: Bishop states that body weight was NOT fully supported by aerodynamic force and that some of the lift went into forward acceleration. The angles of attack are far above where an engineered wing stalls. Bishop KL 2006 (J Exp Biol 209:689-701, doi 10.1242/jeb.02062) reports the same for Glaucomys volans, gliding at 35.4-53.5 deg with the wings stalled and accelerating downward, and finds flying squirrels reach higher lift coefficients than sugar gliders -- so 1.48 is, if anything, generous for a mammal without a flying squirrel's specialisations.

entries.author: agent:flying-mouse
entries.body: generation 2: Generation 1 is short by a factor of 2.6 and the check named both ways out: 180 cm2 of membrane at a jump launch, or 4.8 m/s at the 70 cm2 proposed. The second has a precedent -- Bishop 2006 launched flying squirrels from 4 m, and a 4 m drop is worth about 8.9 m/s before drag -- so this generation stops asking the mouse to jump into flight and lets it fall into a glide. That is a change to the question as much as to the animal, and it is recorded as one.

entries.author: agent:flying-mouse
entries.body: the coefficient that produced this verdict was measured on gliding mammals that were NOT supporting their own weight. Bishop 2007 (doi 10.1242/jeb.002071) reports Petaurus breviceps accelerating downward at 1.0 +/- 0.5 m/s2 in the same glides the 1.48 came from, and states that body weight was not fully supported by aerodynamic force. So "carries" here means the steady-state inequality closes at an airspeed only a fall can supply, using a coefficient borrowed from animals that were themselves descending.

entries.author: agent:flying-mouse
entries.body: generation 3: Generation 2 closed the inequality by letting the animal fall. That is a glide, and the question was flight -- wings that SUPPORT it. So ask the check the question as posed, with powered flight stated, and see whether it has the decency to refuse.

entries.author: agent:flying-mouse
entries.body: asked about powered flight it refuses, and says why the refusal is not pedantry: the question asked is about POWERED flight, and this check cannot answer it. It compares lift with weight at a given airspeed, which is an area question; powered flight is a power question -- whether the flight muscle can supply the induced and profile power through a wingbeat, continuously, at that animal's mass. That needs a coefficient measured through a wingbeat and a muscle power density for the clade, and this repository has neither.

what_is_missing: a lift coefficient measured through a wingbeat cycle, not in a steady glide
a mass-specific mechanical power output for the flight muscle of this clade
a wingbeat frequency and amplitude, or a measurement to fix them
detail.what_this_can_answer: whether lift carries weight at a stated airspeed, which is a necessary condition for flight of any kind, and so a lower bound on the question asked.

conflicts.label: patagium
conflicts.axiom: Uberon asserts never_in_taxon "Glires" for "patagium" (on the term, a superclass, or a whole it is part of), and the NCBI taxonomy places Mus musculus inside that clade.

counterexamples.reading: "patagium" is asserted never_in_taxon Glires. Pteromyini is inside that clade, and this repository's own inventory writes its common name as "Pteromyini", "flying squirrels", "flying squirrels" -- a name for flight. Either that name is wrong or the axiom is too wide. This tool does not decide which.

honesty.mesh: No generation of this animal has a surface mesh. anatomy-model/parametric is a parametric TELEOST builder and Blender is not installed on the machine this ran on, so no .glb was built and none is shown. The 3D view draws the ONTOLOGY HIERARCHY -- which structures the design has and what contains what -- and that is structure without shape: it cannot be flown, measured for area, or printed.
honesty.declared: The mass, membrane area and airspeed in generations 1-3 are DESIGN INPUTS. Each carries a source string saying so. Nobody has measured a winged mouse and nothing here pretends otherwise.
honesty.verdicts: Every verdict on this page is the string the tool itself returned, with the numbers it returned, copied from the session log. Nothing is recomputed here and nothing is rounded for display except where the page shows a fixed number of decimals.
